title: What Is the 'Korea Discount'? Why Korean Stocks Look Cheap
html:
Korea makes some of the world's most valuable chips, cars and ships. Yet for years its stock market has been described with a phrase that sounds like a sale sign: the Korea discount (코리아 디스카운트).

In one line

The Korea discount is the tendency of South Korean companies to trade at lower stock-market valuations than similar companies in other countries.

How big is the gap?

The usual yardstick is the price-to-book ratio (P/B), which compares a company's market value with the value of its net assets. A P/B below 1 means the market values the company at less than its own books say it is worth.

  • The Korea Economic Institute of America says KOSPI companies averaged a P/B of about 0.99 from 2014 to 2024, compared with about 1.8 in Japan and 3.7 in the United States.
  • A June 2026 column in The Korea Times reported that 68.2% of KOSPI companies traded below book value, against 1.9% for the S&P 500 and about 22% for Japan's Nikkei 225.

Where the word comes from

The phrase is Konglish-style financial shorthand used by Korean and foreign investors alike. No single person is credited with coining it. It simply describes the "discount" investors apply when they price Korean shares.

Why the discount exists

  • Family control: in most large Korean companies, one family or shareholder effectively runs the business while owning far less than half of it, often through chains of affiliates (see our post on chaebol).
  • Low payouts: Korean firms have historically paid out less of their profits as dividends and buybacks.
  • Inheritance tax: high inheritance tax gives some families a reason to prefer low share prices.
  • Geopolitics: tension with North Korea is often mentioned as part of the risk investors price in.

In the news

The government has been trying to close the gap. In February 2024 the Financial Services Commission launched the Corporate Value-up Program, encouraging firms to publish plans to raise their value, and a Korea Value-up Index followed in October 2024. On November 1, 2026, the Korea Exchange named 151 companies (96 on KOSPI and 55 on Kosdaq) with persistently low P/B ratios, including Hanwha Life, Hyundai Steel and Lotte Shopping. The list stays public until May 2027 and will be updated every May and November.

Don't confuse it with

  • Korea premium: the hoped-for opposite, when Korean stocks would trade above their peers.
  • Kimchi premium: a different idea from crypto markets, when Bitcoin trades higher on Korean exchanges than abroad.

This article is general information, not investment advice.

Sources

  • Korea Economic Institute of America: Explaining South Korea's Stock Market Boom (July 2026)
  • The Korea Times: 'Korea discount' still persists despite chip-driven rallies (June 2026)
  • The Korea Times: 151 firms flagged for persistently low valuations (Nov 1, 2026)
